extra.message: DocumentController.render() (DocumentController.java:104-109) passes the raw, client-supplied multipart filename (file.getOriginalFilename()) straight into DocumentRenderService.toPdf() as `fileName`, which is then concatenated unescaped into a single command string executed via `new ProcessBuilder("cmd", "/c", "soffice --headless --convert-to pdf " + fileName)`. Because the whole command is parsed by cmd.exe (not passed as separate argv entries), shell metacharacters in the filename (e.g. `& calc.exe`, `| whoami`, `> out.txt`) are interpreted by the shell, giving an authenticated applicant full OS command injection / RCE on the document-conversion host. Unlike DocumentStorage.store(), which sanitizes the filename before use, this path never sanitizes it.

partnerIntake() Base64-decodes the attacker-controlled `X-Intake-State` header and feeds it directly into `new ObjectInputStream(...).readObject()` with no class allow-list or filter. Java native deserialization of untrusted bytes is a well-known RCE primitive (gadget chains in libraries such as commons-collections present on the classpath). Critically, `/api/integration/partner/**` is listed in SecurityConfig.PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS, so this endpoint is reachable with no authentication at all.

noticePreview() takes the `wording` query parameter directly from the request and evaluates it as a Velocity template via `Velocity.evaluate(context, writer, "officerNotice", wording)`. Apache Velocity templates can invoke arbitrary Java via `#set($x=$class.inspect(...))`/`.getClass()` reflection gadgets, so an authenticated officer-role caller can achieve server-side template injection leading to remote code execution.

estimateLimit() reads the `mb_limit_rule` cookie value verbatim and passes it to `org.mvel2.MVEL.executeExpression(expression, vars)`. MVEL expressions can call arbitrary Java methods/constructors (e.g. `Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)` via reflection), and the cookie is fully client-controlled (any site can set it, or the user can edit it directly), so this is a direct remote-code-execution sink driven by untrusted input.

importLegacyBranchFeed() parses attacker-influenced `xml` (from the request body) with a plain `new com.thoughtworks.xstream.XStream()` and no security framework / type permissions configured (`XStream.setupDefaultSecurity` / allow-list is never called). Default-configured XStream is a documented RCE vector (e.g. CVE-2013-7285/CVE-2021-21341-class gadget chains) since it can instantiate arbitrary classes from the XML. This is distinct from, and far weaker than, the hardened SecureReferenceXmlParser used elsewhere in the same controller.

partnerDecision() parses the `X-Partner-Assertion` header with `Jwts.parserBuilder().build().parseClaimsJwt(assertion)`, which is the JJWT API for an UNSIGNED (plain) JWT — it performs no signature verification. Combined with `/api/integration/partner/**` being public (SecurityConfig.PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS), any anonymous caller can forge an assertion with an arbitrary `sub` (application id) and `bureauScore` claim and have it accepted as a trusted partner decision, injecting fabricated bureau scores for any application.

cwe: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

extra.message: setWorkspaceContext() writes the client-supplied `role` (and `email`/`name`) from the JSON request body straight into the HTTP session's ROLE_ATTR/EMAIL_ATTR with no validation against the caller's real identity. SessionAuthFilter.applyPrincipal() (SessionAuthFilter.java:46,62-67) later builds the Spring Security authentication purely from these session attributes (`ROLE_<role>`), which WebSecurityConfig uses for `hasRole("BANK_ADMIN")`-style gates on `/admin/**`, `/officer/**`, `/compliance/**`. Any already-authenticated low-privilege user (e.g. a PROSPECT) can POST `{"role":"bank_admin"}` to this endpoint and have the web tier treat them as BANK_ADMIN for route/menu authorization, bypassing the role checks in WebSecurityConfig.

Desk session references are generated from a simple incrementing `AtomicLong` starting at 1000 ("DESK-1001", "DESK-1002", ...) with no signing or randomness. CommonController.openDesk() (CommonController.java:130-139) lets any authenticated user mint such a session for an arbitrary `role`/`email` request parameter and stores the resulting `mb_desk` cookie value as the sole lookup key in a plain in-memory map (DeskSessionStore.java:17). SessionAuthFilter (SessionAuthFilter.java:48-50) grants the associated role purely from this guessable cookie value with no password or token check, so an attacker can enumerate/guess a desk reference (or just open their own with role=bank_admin via openDesk) to assume another workspace's role.

The CORS mapping for `/customer/**` combines `allowedOriginPatterns("*")` with `allowCredentials(true)`. This permits any origin on the internet to issue credentialed (cookie-bearing) cross-site requests to the customer channel and read the JSON responses, letting a malicious site exfiltrate an authenticated customer's session data (dashboard, re-KYC case state, etc.) via cross-origin fetch with `credentials: 'include'`.

cwe: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

extra.message: searchDirectory() builds the LDAP search filter by directly concatenating the caller-supplied `employeeRef` into `"(&(objectClass=person)(uid=" + employeeRef + "))"` with no escaping of LDAP special characters (`*`, `(`, `)`, `\`, NUL). A crafted `employeeId` (reachable via AdminApiController.staffDirectory, AdminApiController.java:535-542) can inject additional filter clauses or a wildcard to alter the search semantics (LDAP filter injection).

extra.message: searchDepartment() concatenates the caller-supplied `department` parameter directly into the LDAP filter `"(department=" + department + ")"` with no escaping, reachable from StaffDirectoryController.searchStaffByDepartment (StaffDirectoryController.java:35-41). Same LDAP filter injection class as searchDirectory() in this file.

extra.message: searchPolicyRegister() builds an XPath expression by concatenating each CSV row's `identifier` field directly into `"//holder[policyNo='" + identifier + "']"` with no escaping of quote characters. A crafted identifier in the uploaded CSV (e.g. `' or '1'='1`) changes the XPath query logic, allowing an attacker to retrieve policy-holder records they should not match (XPath injection).

extra.message: The client-supplied `fileName` (originalFilename) is used unsanitized in `workDir.resolve(fileName)` / `Files.write(source, content)`. A filename containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../somefile`) can write the uploaded content outside the freshly created temp directory, unlike DocumentStorage.store() which sanitizes the filename and verifies containment before writing.

stageAuditExport() builds `new java.io.File(exportDir.toFile(), fileName)` from the raw `fileName` request parameter with no normalization or containment check against `exportDir`. A value such as `../../../../etc/cron.d/evil` lets an authenticated bank-admin write the CSV content to an arbitrary path reachable from the storage root (arbitrary file write via path traversal).

browseStorage() resolves the client-supplied `folder` field against the storage root and normalizes it, but never verifies the result still starts with `root` (unlike PortalDocumentsController.content(), which performs that check). A `folder` value such as `../../../..` lets an admin-authenticated caller list directories anywhere on the filesystem the process can read.

inspectStoredDocument() resolves the client-supplied `reference` field directly against `storageDir` with `Paths.get(storageDir).resolve(reference)` and reads its file attributes, with no normalization or containment check at all. A `reference` such as `../../../../etc/passwd` lets an authenticated officer probe the existence, size and mtime of arbitrary files on the host filesystem.

updateAccountProfile() calls `BeanUtils.copyProperties(form, account)` against the customer's own Account entity using an `AccountProfileForm` that exposes both `product` and `kycTier` fields. `Account.kycTier` is the authoritative value read back by ViewService.java:142 to look up the KycTierPolicy (daily transaction limit / balance ceiling) and by ReKycService, not merely a display label. Despite the method comment describing this as a 'display settings' endpoint, a customer can PATCH an arbitrary `kycTier` string (e.g. "tier_3") directly onto their account, self-escalating their transaction/balance limits without ever passing the real KYC tier derivation or compliance override flow.

cwe: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: EnvelopeCodec uses a hardcoded default AES key (`Meridian-Envelope-Key-2026-000000`, via the `@Value` default) together with a fixed all-zero 16-byte IV (`private static final byte[] IV = new byte[16]`) for every AES/CBC decryption. If the key is left at its default (as many such `@Value` defaults are in practice) or the IV reuse is exploited, this is both a hardcoded-credential and a broken-cryptography weakness: encrypting any two envelopes with the same key/IV pair leaks structural information and makes the scheme vulnerable to standard CBC attacks.

importStaffRoster() takes the CSV-supplied `initial_code` value and stores it as the new staff account's `passwordHash` via `md5Digest(row[6])` (defined at AdminService.java:378-390) — a single unsalted MD5 digest — bypassing the `PasswordEncoder` (BCrypt) used everywhere else in AuthService/AdminService. AuthService.legacyDigestMatches() (AuthService.java:346-363) will subsequently accept logins against this weak digest, so any account provisioned this way has credential storage equivalent to unsalted MD5 instead of BCrypt.

cwe: CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

extra.message: enrolDeskCredential() lets any authenticated officer overwrite their account's `passwordHash` with `deskCredentialHash(deskCode)` (OfficerApiController.java:272-283), an unsalted MD5 digest of a client-supplied `X-Desk-Code` header, instead of going through the BCrypt `PasswordEncoder`. This downgrades that account's credential storage to unsalted MD5 going forward (and is accepted at login via AuthService.legacyDigestMatches()).
